newsitem.title: UK: COBALT CONSUMERS TWITCHY OVER UNCERTAIN SUPPLIES.
newsitem.headline: COBALT CONSUMERS TWITCHY OVER UNCERTAIN SUPPLIES.

text.p: A loss of production at Canada's Falconbridge Ltd Sudbury, Ontario, facility and low levels of nearby stock may ignite a flurry of consumer covering and drive cobalt prices higher by the end of August, several traders suggested on Tuesday.

Others agreed cobalt had potential to move higher but aired caution, saying that the volume of demand so far during the slow summer period was only enough to underpin and stabilise prices rather than, as one put it, "light a fuse wire for a rapid rises."
Traders said global stocks were extremely low and consumers that traditionally cover in the fourth period were becoming sensitive to improved market fundamentals.
"There is a gentle discomfort by consumers in North America as they eye the situation at Falconbridge," one said.
Workers at Sudbury have been on strike since August 1. The facility produced 1,600 tonnes of cobalt, including custom feed, in 1996.
One source said that five tonnes a day is being lost due to the strike.
"Consumers in the U.S. and Canada are twitching," the trader added.
Usually during the slow summer period in the Northern Hemisphere consumers can find enough material to meet their requirements.
"But with Falconbridge closed the security blanket of supply is been pulled down," a trader commented.
"They (consumers) are not fully exposed at the moment as it is believed that Falconbridge holds some stock, though an extended strike will severely damage the supply-demand outlook," one source said.
The strike comes against the backdrop of low production from producers Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
Traders' stocks are also believed to be minimal.
One trader estimated that stocks held world-wide was around 1,000 tonnes, compared with approximately 18,000 tonnes at the end of 1993.
He suggested short-term prices had the power to drive three or four dollars above current levels, "fundamentals justify such a move."
The trader estimated the stocks/weeks consumption ratio is currently at critical levels at around two-weeks.
With the brisk fourth quarter fast approaching supply and demand will become a major concern to the market.
"There will not be enough metal to satisfy the market...there is going to be a huge short-fall," a trader commented.

Traders will also continue to eye cobalt stockpile sales from the U.S. Defense Logistics Agency (DLA). The August tender of around 500,000 pounds of material was oversubscribed by nearly five times the amount on offer.
Bids totalled more than 2.4 million pounds.
The DLA is likely to tender between 500,000 and 600,000 tonnes of cobalt in September, below the expected 1.5 million pounds, traders said.
In late afternoon trading on Tuesday high grade cobalt was indicated around $23.00/$24.00 a pound, while Russian ingot was pegged at $19.80/$20.80.
-- Paul Shannon, London Newsroom +44 171 542-8075
